key_facts: **Palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP)** is a chronic, relapsing eruption of sterile yellow pustules on the palms and soles that turn brown and scale.
Strongly linked to **smoking** (most patients smoke or have smoked); mainly women aged 40–60.
Distinct from palmoplantar psoriasis, though some have psoriasis elsewhere.
Stop smoking; very potent topical steroid (clobetasol) ± occlusion; refer for hand–foot PUVA, acitretin or other systemics.
Screen for thyroid disease and coeliac disease if symptomatic; SAPHO (bone pain) is a rare association.

ul: chronic relapsing **sterile** pustular eruption confined to palms/soles; now regarded as **distinct from psoriasis** (different genetics — not linked to PSORS1/HLA-C*06; IL-36/IL-17/IL-8 pathways), though ~10–25% also have plaque psoriasis. Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau = digit-tip variant.
psoriasis localised to palms/soles, alone or with plaques elsewhere; disproportionately disabling (manual tasks, walking).

sub: Women 3–4× more often; peak 40–60; uncommon (about 1 in 1,000–10,000).

ul: adults 20–60, **women ≈ 4:1**, **70–90% current/ex-smokers** (nicotinic receptors on eccrine ducts); associations: thyroid disease, coeliac disease, diabetes, psoriatic arthritis, SAPHO/sternoclavicular osteitis; drug-induced by **TNF-α inhibitors**.
trauma/friction (Koebner — manual work), infection, stress, lithium, β-blockers, smoking, alcohol, obesity.
Smoking (nicotine receptors on eccrine sweat ducts), genetics (IL-36 pathway), focal infection; thyroid autoimmunity.
**"The pustules are infected"**: they are sterile; antibiotics do not help.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: PPP begins in the **eccrine sweat duct**, where neutrophils gather into sterile pustules.

mech.t: Nicotine and other triggers activate the acrosyringium (top of the sweat duct).
Vesicle → yellow pustule → brown macule → scale.
mech.caption: PPP lesions evolve from vesicle to pustule to brown scale.

mech.t: Central palms, thenar and hypothenar eminences, heels and insteps.
mech.caption: Typical PPP sites.

histo: Intraepidermal unilocular pustule filled with neutrophils, near the eccrine duct.

ul: crops of 1–10 mm yellow pustules on thenar/hypothenar eminences, central palms, insteps, heels → dry to **brown "rusty" macules**; scale, fissures; burning/pain > itch; symmetrical.

(1) well-defined red scaly plaques; (2) diffuse thick hyperkeratosis without much redness (acquired keratoderma). Painful **fissures**; sharp border; symmetrical. More frequent **nail psoriasis** and **psoriatic arthritis** — screen (PEST questionnaire).

ddx.f: Fever, sheets of pustules beyond hands and feet: emergency.

ul: hyperkeratotic hand eczema (hardest — biopsy or patch testing sometimes needed; they can coexist), tinea (scrape), KE, PPP, keratoderma.

**smoking cessation** (strongest modifiable factor; refer to stop-smoking service/NRT); emollients; **very potent TCS** (clobetasol) ± occlusion overnight; salicylic acid for scale. Refer: hand–foot PUVA, **acitretin**, methotrexate, ciclosporin; biologics less reliable than in psoriasis. Screen thyroid/coeliac if symptomatic.

emollients and keratolytics (salicylic acid 2–5%, urea); **potent/very potent TCS** ± vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) or combination products; occlusion overnight; lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, weight). Refer (CKS/NICE CG153): hand–foot PUVA, acitretin, methotrexate, ciclosporin, apremilast and biologics per NICE psoriasis TAs.

ladder.t: **Stop smoking**: the strongest modifiable factor; stop-smoking service / NRT. Emollients; salicylic acid 2–5% or urea for scale.
**Very potent TCS** (clobetasol) ± overnight occlusion for PPP. Psoriasis: potent / very potent TCS ± calcipotriol or combination product.
Hand–foot **PUVA**, **acitretin**, methotrexate, ciclosporin. Apremilast and biologics per NICE psoriasis TAs; biologics less reliable in PPP.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Antibiotics**: Pustules are sterile: antibiotics don’t help.

refer.t: Fever with sheets of pustules beyond hands and feet: **generalised pustular psoriasis**.
Can’t work or walk: early dermatology referral.
Not responding to very potent steroid and smoking cessation.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Fever with sheets of pustules beyond the hands and feet: **generalised pustular psoriasis**, emergency.
Inability to work or walk: early dermatology referral.
Pustules on one foot only, or with interdigital scale: scrape for **tinea**.
Pain, fissures, difficulty walking and working; impaired quality of life.
Chronic, with remission in some after stopping smoking.

pearls: Smoking cessation is the single most effective change in PPP; offer stop-smoking support at every visit.
Use very potent steroids under cling-film or cotton-glove occlusion at night for short periods, then step down.
Tell patients the pustules are **sterile**: antibiotics do not help.
Screen for psoriatic arthritis (PEST) and ask about chest-wall pain (SAPHO).

quiz.q: Single biggest modifiable factor in PPP?
quiz.a: Smoking: 70–90% are current or ex-smokers; stopping helps most.

quiz.q: Pustules on one foot with interdigital scale?
quiz.a: Scrape for tinea before labelling PPP.

quiz.q: Fever and sheets of pustules spreading off the hands?

quiz.a: Very potent topical steroid (e.g. clobetasol) ± overnight occlusion, plus emollient.
